title: Could Digitalisation Change Fashion's Production Model?
description: Read article about This article examines how digital try-ons, pre-orders, and 3D production could shift fashion from forecasts towards demand-led orders and affect suppliers. and more articles about Textile industry at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Digital try-ons, body scanning, and pre-orders could let brands test demand before cutting fabric, shifting some production from forecasts towards confirmed orders.
The shift may reduce unsold stock and fit-related returns, but it will not automatically lower consumption if brands use faster feedback loops to launch more styles.
Suppliers will need paid flexibility.
markdown:
Imagine this. It is lunchtime, and a shopper is sitting at her desk, phone in hand. She opens her favourite brand’s product page, uploads a photo of herself and watches a knitted jacket appear on her. She turns the 3D image of herself, checks the length against her hips and wonders whether she prefers the navy to the red. She settles on navy and taps to order.

The jacket she has just tried on does not yet exist: not in navy, not in her size and not in any warehouse. For now, it is simply a 3D file made up of a pattern, a fabric simulation and a price.

For most of fashion’s history, this sequence has run the other way round. Clothes have been made first and sold second: designed, cut and sewn in their thousands and shipped across the world. These designs are then put in front of shoppers in the hope that enough of them will sell.

But what if the sale came before the materialisation of the product?

Online shopping is a huge industry, and 3D changing rooms already exist. Shoppers browse, compare and try on through a screen, while brands can create garments realistic enough to sell before any fabric is cut. These evolving capabilities raise the questions: if a garment can be shown first and made later, could fashion move from producing on a forecast to producing on demand? And if so, what would that mean for the mills and factories that make the clothes?

## Fashion’s Educated Guess

The current mass-production model is dependent on forecasting. Months before a collection reaches the shops, a brand has to decide how many units of each style to order, in which colours and in which sizes. These decisions are locked in early due to manufacturing economics. Fabric is bought by the roll, dyed by the batch and cut in stacked layers, so the cost of each garment falls as the order grows. Factories set a minimum order quantity for the same reason: a line that has to be reset for every few hundred pieces loses time and money with each change. The result is a system that efficiently makes clothes but still relies on guesswork about how many people will buy them, like them and keep them rather than send them back.

When a forecast is too cautious, a brand sells out and misses sales. When it is too optimistic, the surplus is marked down, moved on through outlets and secondary markets or, in some cases, never sold at all. The European Environment Agency (EEA) estimates that between 4 and 9 per cent of all textile products placed on the European market are destroyed before they are ever used, between 264,000 and 594,000 tonnes a year1.

Things are changing. Since July 19, 20262, large companies in the EU have been banned from destroying unsold clothing, clothing accessories and footwear under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR). Destruction covers recycling and incineration as well as landfill3. Unsold items must instead be sold, donated or prepared for reuse. Medium-sized companies have until 2030 to comply.

The ban does not stop a brand ordering too much. It does, however, give brands good reason to be more cautious.

## The Shopper Has Already Gone Digital

While production still runs on forecasts, shopping has moved on. A growing share of clothing is chosen on a screen, and the tools for this are becoming more sophisticated. In December 2025, Google brought its virtual try-on tool to shoppers in the UK and India4, letting them see billions of apparel listings on themselves by uploading a single photo. Smartphone body scanning and online size finders work towards the same goal from a different angle, turning a shopper’s body into data that can be matched against a garment.

The reason retailers are investing in these tools is the return. According to the EEA5, around one in five garments bought online is sent back, and around 70 per cent of those returns come down to how the item looks or fits on the buyer. Before the ban, the agency estimated that between 22 and 43 per cent of returned clothing was destroyed rather than resold, often because checking, cleaning and repackaging it cost more than the item was worth.

Part of the problem is that sizing is inconsistent. A ‘medium’ from one brand can fit like a ‘small’ from another, which is why many shoppers order more than one size and send the rest back. A 2025 study of returns data from one of the UK’s largest online-only fashion retailers6, found that between 14.5 and 17 per cent of returns, depending on the department, came from ‘bracketing’ (ordering several sizes or colours of the same item to try on at home).

This is more than a retail problem for the supplier. Every returned garment was cut, sewn and shipped to meet a sale that never happened. The information that would have prevented it, whether the shopper was a size 10 or 12, whether she preferred the navy or the red, was only captured after the event.

This is what is starting to change. Digital shopping could now be used to create a detailed picture of what people want, and what fits them, before purchasing. Try-on sessions, abandoned baskets, size selections and wish lists all point to demand that has not yet turned into an order. For now, most of that information stays with retailers and their marketing teams. But what if it travels further up the supply chain, to the point where production decisions are made.

## Show it First, Make it Later

The first signs of that shift are already visible. In wholesale, virtual showrooms allow buyers to view and order collections from 3D samples rather than physical ones, meaning the order book can take shape before sampling is complete. In retail, some brands now open pre-orders on new styles and only commit to production once enough customers have paid, turning a forecast into something closer to a confirmed order.

At the more radical end sits the US company Unspun, which began by selling custom-fit jeans made from body scans. Its founders found that the hardest problem was not measuring the customer but making a one-off garment affordably. Their answer is a 3D weaving machine that goes straight from yarn to garment, skipping the stages of weaving flat fabric, cutting it and sewing it together. Walmart began piloting the technology in 2024, starting with men’s chinos7, and Decathlon signed a partnership with the company later that year8. The company’s aim is a network of small, local production sites that make clothing when it is ordered rather than months in advance. The garments produced so far have been simple woven styles such as trousers, so there is still a gap from covering the full wardrobe.

The consumer obstacle is patience. Shoppers have been trained to expect next-day delivery, and made-to-order clothing asks them to wait. There is some evidence that they will, if given a reason. A 2024 study of online fashion shoppers in German-speaking countries9, published in Transportation Research Part D, found that willingness to wait rose markedly when customers were offered savings on delivery or shown the emissions a slower option would avoid.

Even so, made-to-order is unlikely to suit every category. It works best where fit matters and styles change slowly, such as denim, tailoring and workwear. For trend-driven pieces bought on impulse, the wait may be enough to lose the sale.

Distance adds to the wait. Much of the world’s clothing is made in countries such as Bangladesh and India, far from many of the shoppers who buy it. A factory there cannot make and post one jacket at a time at a sensible cost, so orders would need to be gathered into small batches before production starts and shipped together once they are finished. Unless customers are buying on a clear pre-order basis, knowing they will wait, that delay is hard to justify.

There is a wider risk too. Garments make up more than 80 per cent of Bangladesh’s export earnings and employ over four million people10. Factories like these were built for volume. If orders become smaller and less predictable, or move closer to Western markets, they could lose work, and the pressure on price could grow.

## Smaller Batches, Same Volume?

It would be easy to assume that producing closer to demand means producing less. The most successful example of demand-led manufacturing so far suggests otherwise.

Shein built its business on a test-and-repeat model. According to reporting by the Chinese business outlet 36Kr11, first orders at its supplier factories typically run to just 100 to 200 pieces. Styles are released online in small quantities, sales data is watched in real time, and only the designs that perform are reordered at scale. It is, in many ways, the digital production model described above: design fast, show it to the market, and make more only once demand is proven.

However, the result has not been a smaller fashion industry. The same model that keeps unsold stock low per style has allowed Shein to release new designs at a pace traditional retailers cannot match, and to grow into one of the largest fashion retailers in the world. A small first order does not mean a small total: a style that sells can be reordered many times over. For its suppliers, the model has meant a constant stream of short runs rather than fewer, larger orders, a pattern that could spread as other brands adopt similar tools.

So, digital tools can reduce the waste that comes from guessing wrong, but they do not decide how much clothing the world buys. A system that responds perfectly to demand will also respond perfectly to demand that is growing. Whether digitalisation leads to more responsible production or simply faster consumption depends on how brands use it.

## What it Asks of Suppliers

For mills and factories, the direction of travel matters more than the pace. Even a partial move towards demand-led production changes what brands will ask of their suppliers.

1. Smaller, Faster, Less Predictable Orders: Orders placed against confirmed demand tend to be smaller and more frequent, with less notice. A factory used to planning around a handful of large seasonal orders may instead receive a steady flow of short runs and repeat orders that depend on how a style is selling that week. Planning, staffing and buying raw materials all become harder when the order book changes from one week to the next.

2. The Economics of the Minimum Order: Short runs mean more changeovers, and every changeover costs time. Suppliers will need to decide how low their minimums can go, and how to price flexibility rather than absorb it. Factories that can switch lines quickly and still make a margin on a few hundred pieces will be better placed than those built only for volume. Digital tools can help here, as accurate 3D patterns and automated cutting reduce the set-up time for each new style.

3. Holding Fabric, Dyeing Later: If brands delay decisions on colour and quantity, the pressure moves upstream to the mill. One response is to hold fabric in an undyed state and dye it once orders are confirmed, so that stock can be turned into whichever colour is selling. Mills that offer stock-supported fabric programmes can become valuable partners to brands trying to shorten their commitments. The trade-off is that the mill holds stock for longer, which ties up cash.

4. Data as Part of the Service: Demand-led production only works if information moves quickly in both directions. Shein, for example, provides its supplier factories with digital systems that track order progress and sales data in real time. Suppliers who are able to work from 3D files, share live production updates, and respond to sales signals will find it easier to win this kind of business. Over time, such digital capability may become a basic requirement for suppliers rather than a way to stand out.

5. Distance and Risk: Speed favours proximity, which could strengthen the case for producing closer to major markets. It also raises a harder question: when a brand stops guessing how much to order, who carries the risk? Somebody still has to hold fabric and keep capacity available. Suppliers will want to make sure that flexibility is paid for, rather than simply passed down the chain. Longer-term agreements on capacity, instead of one-off orders, may be one way to share that risk more fairly.

## From Forecast to Order

The jacket on the shopper’s phone is a small thing, but it points to a shift in where production decisions begin. For decades, the process started with a forecast and ended with a sale. Digital tools make it possible, at least for some products, to start with the sale instead.

Whether that becomes the norm will depend on shoppers’ patience, the economics of short runs and how honestly brands use the data they gather. What is already clear is that the suppliers best placed for this future will be those able to make small quantities well, quickly and profitably.

Fashion has spent decades learning how to make clothes at scale. The next test may be making them at the right scale.
author: Scarlett Buckley
